They immediately refer patients to specialists if their symptoms are beyond their initial diagnosis, never neglecting a patient's condition. (For example, one friend's mother almost had a stroke. This clinic, run by these two doctors, is a beloved haven for the underprivileged. The treatment and medication costs are very reasonable compared to many other clinics, which is why so many patients choose this clinic.

text:
🩺 How a Thai doctor saved me from pain that they couldn't cure in Russia:

The story began long before Thailand. Back in Russia, I felt a strange, nagging pain in my right upper quadrant. It was alarming, especially as I was preparing to move. I was seriously scared, feared the worst, and went for a full checkup.

I donated blood. Had an ultrasound. Swallowed a tube with a camera. Everything was fine. The only thing they found was Helicobacter pylori bacteria in my stomach lining. I was prescribed a course of antibiotics. I took everything exactly as prescribed, but the pain didn't go away. It would subside, then return.

Then one day in Thailand, this time in Pattaya, I felt a sharp cramp again. I decided to go to a Thai clinic in the hopes of finally figuring out what was going on.

My insurance didn't cover routine visits—only emergency ones. I knew that if I went to a private hospital like Bangkok Hospital, I'd shell out at least 10,000 baht just for the appointment and the pills. So the choice was obvious. I went to the public clinic, Banglamung Hospital, where my friend had gotten an X-ray, a cast, and all the necessary medications for a mere 1,700 baht when he broke his arm.

But this time, when I went in person, I had no idea what to do. The ticket machine wasn't working. The display was blank. Everything was in Thai. I stood there, lost in the middle of the hall, wondering where to go or who to see.

Luckily, a Thai woman waiting in line with her son helped me. I told her what was bothering me. She went to find out which doctor I needed to see and returned with the news: the doctor I needed was no longer available that day. But she told me that the same doctor was available after work at a private clinic—literally a five-minute walk away.

I decided to go there, got a number, and waited until it opened. It was my first visit to such a small Thai clinic. And, frankly, I was amazed by the atmosphere. The strawberry-colored wooden ottomans at the entrance—it was like something out of a fairy tale. And inside, everything was very simple, cozy, and cozy.

The doctor looked me in the eyes, listened carefully, gently touched my stomach—and that was it. No tests, no ultrasound. He said I had a gallbladder spasm. Apparently, it was caused by nerves. He prescribed two medications—and that was it. I took a two-week course, and the pain went away forever.

I was amazed then at how accurately the doctor diagnosed me without any equipment. Just from experience.

In Russia, I had undergone countless tests, wasted time and money—but no one could figure out the cause of the pain. And here, they simply helped me… by feeling my stomach with their hands.

I'm not saying in any way that our doctors are worse. Russian medicine has saved me more than once in the most difficult situations. Something just went wrong this time.

And what's surprising is that I paid pennies for the clinic appointment. It was such a small amount that I don't even remember it.
